1338.title: A Protestant service
1338.hook: many Protestant services center on the sermon and hymns
1338.howItsDone: Protestant services vary widely; they often center on Bible readings, a sermon and congregational singing, from traditional hymns to contemporary worship songs, with communion every week in some churches and monthly or quarterly in others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shape of the Mass: gathering, word, table, sending, like the road to Emmaus. Your line was gather, hear, eat, go.

An upstairs room in a town called Troas, lamps burning, people packed in. Paul is leaving in the morning, so he keeps talking. Acts says he "continued his speech until midnight." A young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window. "And as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead." Paul goes down, wraps his arms around him, and says, "Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him." The boy lives. Then, Acts says, Paul goes back upstairs, breaks bread, eats, and keeps talking till daybreak.
screen: `A BOY FALLS ASLEEP IN THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Protestant churches come in a wide range: Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, nondenominational and more, and their services differ. But three things often stand near the center. First, the Bible open. Often it's read aloud, and people follow along in their own copies or on their phones. Paul gives one reason: "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." So the word is read out, in the people's own language, every week. Second, the sermon. In some churches the pulpit stands right in the middle of the front, where everyone's eyes go. The preacher takes a passage and opens it up: what it said then, what it might say now. For Protestants who stress preaching, this is where God speaks to the gathered church: the word preached. Third, the singing. Paul writes, "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." In a hymn, the whole room preaches back. Old hymns with four verses and a choir, new songs with a band and words on a screen: both are trying to put the word in people's mouths. And the table? It's there too. Some Protestant churches share communion every Sunday, others monthly, or a few times a year, and it's often simple and quiet. So if the Mass walks four movements slowly, a Protestant service often leans its weight on one: the word, read, sung and preached.

Bring to mind a hymn or song you know by heart, from church, school or anywhere, and instead of singing it, say the words slowly, as if someone were teaching them to you. Find one line that teaches something. If you pray, offer that line back to God as your own prayer; if not, let the words be just words for a minute, and hear what they say.
A Protestant service. Worship that often centers on the Bible read aloud, the sermon and the singing, with the Lord's table kept weekly in some churches and less often in others.
Your line: the word preached. Faith, Paul says, comes by hearing. Until tomorrow.

1339.title: A Quaker meeting
1339.hook: no minister, no music, only silence and occasional words
1339.howItsDone: In an unprogrammed Quaker meeting for worship, Friends sit together in silence, and anyone who feels moved may stand and speak briefly; other Friends' churches hold programmed worship with pastors, hymns and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Protestant service: the word read, preached and sung, and a boy asleep in the window. Your line was the word preached.

Benches set in a square, facing each other. No pulpit, no altar, no organ. Maybe a small table in the middle with flowers and a Bible. People come in quietly and sit down, and then nothing happens, for a long time. A clock ticks. Someone shifts on the bench. Twenty people, sitting still, saying nothing, together. Then, maybe halfway through, an older man stands up, says three sentences about his granddaughter and a verse he can't stop thinking about, and sits down again. The silence closes back over. This is worship too.

Quakers call themselves the Religious Society of Friends, and their worship a meeting. In the form described here, called unprogrammed, there's no minister and no plan. Friends speak of something of God in everyone, so anyone in the room may be the one given words to say. Some weeks a few people speak; some weeks nobody does. First, the waiting. Friends aren't trying to empty their minds; they're listening. A psalm puts it plainly: "Be still, and know that I am God." Second, the voice. When Elijah hides in a cave, God tells him to stand on the mountain. "But the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice." Not the loud things. The small one, after. Friends wait for that. Third, the speaking. If someone feels truly moved, they stand, speak briefly, and sit. That's called ministry. Others don't answer or argue; they let the words settle into the quiet. Fourth, the gathering. Sometimes, Friends say, the silence changes. It stops being twenty people sitting alone and becomes one people listening together: a gathered meeting. Jesus said, "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Not every Quaker church works this way; some Friends' churches have pastors, hymns and sermons. But in the silent meeting, the gift is a stillness shared.
screen: `NO PLAN: ANYONE MAY BE GIVEN WORDS.`
`NOT THE WIND: A STILL SMALL VOICE.`

segments.voice: If someone's near you, ask if they'll sit quietly with you for two minutes; if you're alone, remember that other people somewhere are sitting in silence right now, and sit with them that way. Don't fill the quiet; if a sentence rises that feels worth keeping, notice it and let it rest. If you pray, you can wait for the still small voice.
A Quaker meeting. Worship in shared silence, with no minister and no plan, where anyone moved to speak may stand and say a few words.
Your line: the gathered silence. Many people, one stillness, nobody in a hurry to fill it. See you tomorrow.

1340.title: A Pentecostal service
1340.hook: long praise, open prayer, testimony, altar call
1340.howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic churches typically hold long times of sung praise with raised hands, open prayer in which some pray in tongues, testimonies from members and an altar call inviting people forward for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Quaker meeting: a still small voice, and silence closing back over. Your line was the gathered silence.

The drummer counts in, and the room is already on its feet. A song starts and keeps going, the same chorus again and again, louder, then softer, then louder. Hands go up all over the room. A woman near the front is crying, and smiling. Somebody shouts amen in the middle of a line. Then the pastor says, let's pray, and the whole room prays out loud at once, every voice saying something different, a wave of sound. Yesterday's room waited in silence. This one waits with everything it's got.
screen: `THE ROOM IS ALREADY ON ITS FEET.`

segments.voice: Pentecostal churches take their name from a day in the book of Acts. The followers of Jesus are together in one place. "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting." Then "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Pentecostals expect that same Spirit in the room today. First, long praise: not one hymn but a stretch of singing, often with hands raised, sometimes with dancing. A psalm gives the reason: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Second, open prayer: many voices praying aloud together, and some praying in tongues, a prayer language they understand as a gift of the Spirit. Other Christians understand the gift of tongues differently, and some believe it belonged to the earliest church. Pentecostals hold that it's for now. Third, testimony. Someone stands and tells what God has done for them this week: a healing, a job, a night they didn't drink. Ordinary people with a microphone, telling the truth. Fourth, the altar call. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who wants prayer, or wants to give their life to Christ, to come to the front, and others gather round, lay hands on them and pray. Behind it all stands a line Jesus said to Nicodemus: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." Wind you can hear, but can't hold.
screen: `A ROOM, A WIND, AND OTHER TONGUES.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a song of praise from any church you like; if not, hum, or breathe out slowly a few times. Let your body join in somehow, hands open on your knees or lifted a little, whatever feels honest. If you pray, thank God out loud for one thing; if not, say aloud one thing you're glad of today.
A Pentecostal service. Worship named for the day of Pentecost, expecting the Spirit to move in the room.
Your line: the spirit moves. Everything that has breath gets to join in. Same time tomorrow.

1341.title: The sermon
1341.hook: Catholics and Orthodox call it a homily; Protestants often a sermon
1341.howItsDone: At Catholic Mass and the Orthodox Divine Liturgy, a priest or deacon gives a homily on the readings just proclaimed; in Protestant services the sermon, often longer, is usually preached by the pastor and frequently stands at the center of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Pentecostal service: long praise, and a wind you hear but can't hold. Your line was the spirit moves.

A Sabbath day in Nazareth, his hometown. Jesus goes to the synagogue, as Luke says was his custom, and stands up to read. He's handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, finds a place, and reads about good news to the poor and freedom for captives. Then Luke slows everything down. "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Every eye in the room, waiting. He begins with one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears."

Catholics and Orthodox Christians usually call it a homily; Protestants often call it a sermon. Both name the same moment: the scripture has been read, and now someone stands, or sits, to open it up. First, an old shape. Long before Nazareth, in the book of Nehemiah, the people gather in Jerusalem by the water gate to hear the law read aloud, and the text says: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Read it, give the sense, help them understand. That's the job. Second, the words. A homily, in Catholic and Orthodox use, stays close to the readings just heard; it's usually short, and it walks from the page to the table. A sermon, in some Protestant churches, can range more widely, take one passage deep, and run longer; it's often the center of the service, as this block saw a few days ago. Same job, different weight. Third, the listener's part. Jesus told a crowd, "Take heed therefore how ye hear." Preaching isn't finished when the preacher sits down. It's finished when somebody carries something out the door. Fourth, the one line. At Nazareth, Luke gives the heart of it in a single sentence. Homilies run longer than that. But what stays, years later, can be one thing a preacher said: a phrase that landed, a story. So a good way to hear any homily or sermon is to listen for the one line to keep.

Bring back a sermon or homily you've heard, recent or long ago; if none comes, use one of these past few lessons. Ask what it was actually saying, squeeze it into one sentence short enough for a single breath, and say it quietly to yourself, twice. If you pray, hand that line to God and ask for help to live it.
Homily. What Catholics and Orthodox call the talk that opens up the readings just heard; Protestants often call it a sermon.
Your line: one line to keep. Years later, what stays is often a single sentence. Until tomorrow.

1342.title: The creed said together
1342.hook: a whole congregation saying what they believe in one voice
1342.howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and some other churches, the congregation says or sings the Nicene Creed or the Apostles' Creed together during the service; Quakers and some Baptist churches do not recite a creed in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon, and the word homily: the talk that opens up the readings. Your line was one line to keep.

The sermon ends. The whole room stands, with a creak of benches and a shuffle of coats, and the minister begins: "I believe in one God." By the third word, everyone has caught up. Some read from a card. Some have known it since they were small. An old man says every word like he's signing his name. Near the back, a woman pauses at a line she's wrestling with, then picks it up at the next one. One long paragraph, said by a whole room in one voice. Today: the creed said together.

Day two hundred ninety-seven gave the creed its name, from credo, I believe. A creed is a short summary of the faith, said out loud, and Christians trace the habit back to the New Testament. Start with Paul, writing to Corinth. He hands on something he says was handed to him: "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Received, then delivered, like a family recipe nobody wrote alone. Next, the mouth. In Romans, Paul puts belief and speech side by side: "For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Faith isn't only kept inside. It gets said. Then, the room. In some churches the Nicene Creed or the Apostles' Creed is said every Sunday. The old English prayer book has it begin, "I believe." Other churches say, "We believe." Some Christians describe that as leaning on the church on a day when their own faith feels thin: nobody carries every word alone. Not every church recites a creed. Quakers and some Baptist churches, for reasons of conscience, prefer not to make any set words a test. Last, a father in Mark's Gospel. His son is suffering. Jesus tells him all things are possible to the one who believes, and the father cries out: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both halves, in one breath.
screen: `WITH THE MOUTH, NOT ONLY THE HEART.`

segments.voice: If you know a creed, say its opening line out loud, slowly, even alone, and notice what changes when the words leave your mouth; if you don't, read the line on the screen. If you pray, you can add the father's words from Mark: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If belief isn't where you are today, simply listen, and notice which word stays with you.
screen: `I BELIEVE IN ONE GOD THE FATHER ALMIGHTY, MAKER OF HEAVEN AND EARTH.`

1343.title: The peace
1343.hook: peace be with you, and with your spirit: a handshake, hug or bow
1343.howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and some other churches, the congregation exchanges a sign of peace during the service with a handshake, embrace or bow, saying "peace be with you"; where it falls in the service differs from church to church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the creed said together: a whole room in one voice. Your line was we believe.

Hand out, then a tiny pause. Is this a handshake person, a hug person, or a nod-from-across-the-aisle person? In the middle of the service everything stops, and strangers turn to greet each other. A small boy shakes every hand within reach, twice. Two people who snapped at each other in the parking lot meet eyes and have to decide something. A woman in the front bows with her palms together. And the same words go back and forth across the pews: "Peace be with you." "And with your spirit."

It looks like a social break. In the rite it's more: the church making peace with itself before it goes further. Four roots. First, a locked room, the one from day six hundred fifty-two. On the evening of the resurrection, in John's Gospel, the disciples hide behind shut doors, afraid. Jesus stands among them, and his first words are no complaint: "Peace be unto you." A couple of verses later, he says it again. Christians who pass the peace pass on his greeting. Second, the early letters. Near the end of Romans, Paul writes a line that would startle some congregations now: "Salute one another with an holy kiss." Some churches still call this the kiss of peace. In the Orthodox liturgy it comes just before the creed, with a call to love one another so the church can confess its faith with one mind. Third, the gift. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says that if you bring your gift to the altar and remember someone has something against you, "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Some churches place the peace just before the gifts come forward, with that verse in mind. In the Catholic Mass the sign of peace comes later, just before communion. Same gesture, a different place, a meaning in each. Fourth, the hands. A handshake in one country, a bow in another, a hug where everyone knows everyone. The form bends. The words stay.
screen: `A LOCKED ROOM: PEACE BE UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, someone you love or someone you're at odds with, the parking-lot person in your life, and hold their face a moment without arguing with it. Then, silently, wish them peace. If you pray, say the risen Jesus's words over them, peace be unto you; if you don't, simply wish them well and mean it, even a little.
The peace. The moment in a service when people greet one another with Jesus's words, peace be with you, before going on together.
Your line: peace be with you. And with your spirit. Rest well.

1344.title: The offering
1344.howItsDone: In many churches an offering of money is collected during the service, by plate, basket or box, and where communion is celebrated the bread and wine are brought to the table at this point; in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they are carried in procession in the Great Entrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peace: a handshake, a hug or a bow, and the risen Jesus's greeting passed along the pews. Your line was peace be with you.

A wicker basket on the end of a long wooden pole swings down the row, and a little girl drops in a coin she's held so tightly it's warm. Across town, a plate goes hand to hand, and someone slips in an envelope. In a third church, a family carries a plate of bread and a small jug of wine up the center aisle and hands them to the priest. In a fourth, just a box by the door. Different churches, one moment: something is carried forward. Today: the offering.

Two kinds of gift come forward at the offering: money for the church and the poor, and, where communion is celebrated that day, bread and wine for the table, sometimes carried up from the pews. In the Orthodox liturgy they're carried through the church in a slow procession called the Great Entrance. The idea underneath both comes from King David. In First Chronicles, the people have just given freely toward building the temple, gold and silver and more. David doesn't congratulate them. He blesses God: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee." It turns giving inside out. Nothing was theirs to begin with; they hand back what they were handed. Some churches say that line as the gifts come forward, and the Orthodox liturgy, as the bread and wine are lifted up, says something close: thine own of thine own. Then the size of a gift. In Mark, Jesus sits near the temple treasury, watching. Rich people put in much. A poor widow puts in two small coins, and Jesus says, "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." They gave from what they had left over. She gave all she had. And the spirit of it: Paul writes, "God loveth a cheerful giver." Not grudgingly, he says, and not because you have to.
screen: `OF THINE OWN HAVE WE GIVEN THEE.`

segments.voice: Turn your hands palm up on your knees, and let a few things you were given come to mind: this breath, a person who taught you, a meal. Then choose one small gift to pass on, some money, an hour, a meal for a neighbor, and decide it now. If you pray, you can say David's words: all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.
The offering. The moment when gifts and bread are carried forward, handing back to God what Christians say was God's to begin with.
Your line: all things come of thee. Two small coins can be more than all. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: Isn't the offering just the part where church asks for money?
options: Not just that: gifts and bread come forward, handing back to God what was God's to begin with.
Yes; Jesus praised the rich givers most, because their big gifts kept the temple going.
It's only about the bread; money was never part of the offering in any church.
chat.meaning: David says all things come of thee: giving hands back what was given. Money, bread and wine come forward, and the widow's two coins count most.
